newsitem.title: USA: Investment newsletters have cold hands in hot market.
newsitem.headline: Investment newsletters have cold hands in hot market.

text.p: With stocks a skip and jump away from new highs, investors are turning to investment newsletters for advice on whether to be in or out of the market.
But a study of 326 newsletters shows that many of these financial wizards have cold hands when it comes to picking stocks.

A five-year study by Duke University and the University of Utah showed that an investment in the best performing newsletters' strategies in December 1990 would have produced an annual return of 12.6 percent by December 1995, compared with a gain of 16 percent for the study's own investment model.
Many of the financial gurus who typically charge $200 or more per year to give advice on the stock market also fail to beat Wall Street.

"Only 16.5 percent of the newsletters provided valuable investment advice and the large majority did not," said Campbell Harvey, a professor of finance at Duke University's Fuqua School of Business who conducted the study with John Graham, professor of finance at University of Utah's Eccles School of Business.
"With the market at record highs, the advice is a really big deal for investors who need to know whether they should be out of the market or not," he said.
On Friday, the Dow Jones industrial average closed up 82.74 points at 6,855.80, not far from its record closing high of 6,883.90 set on Jan. 21. For the week, it was up 42.71 points.
In January, the index, which tracks 30-blue-chip stocks, was up a total of 365 points as the market again fooled many experts who have been predicting a nasty correction.

"We found that most of these newsletters were beaten by our passive investment strategy that maintained a steady mix of 70 percent stocks and 30 percent Treasury bills for the whole year and we did not fluctuate like the newsletters," Harvey said.
He said the passive strategy had the same risk as the newsletters but the key to the success of the study's model is that "we stayed put and we did not listen to anybody else's advice."
The best newsletters produced annual returns of 3.5 percent above the study's model portfolio while the worst letters had returns that were 20.7 percent below the benchmark portfolio, he said.
Harvey said the most common mistake of the newsletter writers was that they reacted the wrong way to the information that affects the market.
"A little piece of information comes up and they immediately adjust their portfolios when they shouldn't have ... over-reacting or under-reacting," he said.
"The point is that if you want to do market timing and vary the amount of money in the market throughout the year people should not look to investment letters for advice," Harvey said.
Market-timing is Wall Street lingo for investors who jump in and out of the stock market hoping to be in the market when it is going up and to be out when it is going down.

"The majority of the newsletters are the perfect examples of the worse sins of the way to invest," said James P. O'Shaughnessy, president of O'Shaughnessy Capital Management and author of "What works on Wall Street."
"They are populated by people who think way too much of their own opinions and some are story tellers and are from the 'got a hunch, bet a bunch' crowd," he said.

O'Shaughnessy said the newsletters that offer investment strategies that have been tested over long periods of time and have the discipline to implement a strategy without overriding their investment models are the most valuable.

"You have the four horsemen of the investment Apocalypse -- fear, greed and ignorance and hope, " he said. "All but one is emotion and ignorance can be corrected but the other ones are very hard to tame."
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite index ended up 11.31 points to 1,357.71. The index was down 22.14 on the week.

The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 9.41 to a new high of 789.56, leaving that index 3.40 points higher for the week. The American Stock Exchange index edged up 1.58 to 586.61, and was off 1.96 on the week.
